steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
On the ragged edge of Hemsley Point, where the granite cliffs break the Atlantic into white, ragged lace, the old lighthouse stood like a lone exclamation mark against the sky. Its keeper, Elias Rowe, had tended the beacon for forty-three winters—long enough for salt to etch his boots and for rumor to wrap him in stories taller than the tower itself.

Each dusk, Elias climbed the iron-spiral throat of the lighthouse with deliberate care, a brass oil can in one hand and a battered journal in the other. The lantern room greeted him with a hush of glass and brass: six great prisms that bent lamplight into blades capable of cutting fog from twenty nautical miles away. He would polish the lenses until they blazed like patient suns, then set the clockwork to turn, its tick steady as a heartbeat.

Tonight, however, the sea delivered something new. A violet storm front advanced—anvil-shaped, silent, almost respectful—while beneath it a lone dory pitched, its sail torn to ribbons. Through his spyglass Elias saw a boy clinging to the mast, hair plastered across his face like kelp. Instinct moved faster than thought. Elias rang the fog bell thrice, as protocol demanded, then dashed down the stairs, legs remembering youth.

Outside, wind howled like memories of wolves. Elias fought it to reach the signal cannon, an antique kept more for ceremony than rescue. He loaded a distress shell—scarlet flare powder packed above black shot—and fired. The blossom of red exploded over the sea, guiding the boy’s eyes toward the only safe inlet beneath the bluff. Moments later the dory veered, sliding between teeth of rock into calmer water.

By the time Elias guided the shivering stranger up the winding cliff path, the storm had broken. In the lighthouse kitchen, lamplight danced over steaming mugs of tea and walls lined with logbooks; years of storms, saves, and solitude whispered from every page. The boy—no more than sixteen—stammered thanks, but Elias only nodded, as if receiving gratitude on behalf of something larger.

When dawn tiptoed across the ocean, the storm’s wreckage glittered like scattered coins, yet the lighthouse stood unscathed, its keeper already at work cleaning salt from the railing. Another night was logged, another life set back on its course. And as the sun ignited the horizon, Elias Rowe merely turned the page, ready for whatever story the sea would write next.
